title: Circuit Breaker & SLA Fallback Automation Postmortem
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-28 14:00 UTC | Duration: 73 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya, Evan (Redwood) — Daniel, Priya, Tom (HeliosCart)

Summary: quick postmortem on a recent SLA regression that HeliosCart saw when their checkout recommender experienced short eviction bursts. Focus was on the automated circuit-breaker behavior, why fallbacks (hosted vs dedicated) didn't kick as expected, and an action plan to tighten runbook triggers and add telemetry hooks.

Topics: root cause recap; circuit-breaker threshold tuning; SLA fallback automation; log collection gaps; runbook and oncall drills; next steps for pilot of automated rollback/circuit-breaker helper.

Action items (captured in transcript — duplicate in metadata): brief list at end.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna run through the incident timeline and the automation around circuit breakers and SLA fallbacks. Sorry for the brief delay, had calendar overlap.
[00:12] Daniel: No worries, appreciate you making time — we've been, like, heads down, this one hit peak traffic during a promo window and it cascaded.
[00:20] Evan: Quick note — we'll try to keep this technical, capture decisions and concrete asks. If you want the deck, I'll drop the slides and the benchmark sheet after.
[00:28] Priya: That would be great. Oh, and the logs I have show some... uh, timestamp drift between app and inference node, not sure if that matters.
[00:36] Tom: To set context: checkout recommender latency spiked from 60ms p95 to 2.3s p95 for about 9 minutes, error rate up ~6%. Our SLO is 200ms p95, so we tripped a few things.
[00:50] Maya: Got it. Can you walk us through what you saw on the circuit-breaker side? I know you had an automation to route to a smaller model and to a cached fallback, right?
[01:04] Priya: Yes — we have a circuit-breaker lambda that runs on metrics ingestion. It should flip to fallback when backend p95 > 500ms for 30s. But during this incident the metric ingestion lagged, so the breaker kicked late.
[01:18] Daniel: There's an edge-case: our metric pipeline (internal) batches metrics every 45s and then filters; during the spike the batching grew to 90s and the breaker only saw the signal after things were already degraded.
[01:30] Evan: That matches what we saw in the KV cache traces — the KV cache showed heavy eviction around the same time, so cache thrash + delayed metric visibility explains late mitigation.
[01:42] Tom: The fallback path was supposed to downgrade to a quantized smaller model running on dedicated capacity (cheaper, lower throughput) or to the cached prefix response. In practice the A/B routing didn't happen because the routing policy rejected the dedicated node due to healthcheck flapping.
[01:56] Maya: Healthchecks flapping — can you expand? Is this the readiness probe on the dedicated pool, or the region-level load balancer?
[02:02] Priya: The dedicated pool's readiness probe was returning 503s intermittently as the model process was GC-ing after memory pressure. Our auto-heal script restarted pods which caused short 503 windows. The routing policy has a 2 consecutive failure rule — that made it avoid the pool entirely for some minutes.
[02:18] Evan: So two contributing factors: delayed breaker due to metrics latency; routing avoiding the dedicated fallback due to transient readiness failures.
[02:26] Daniel: Right, and the worst part — the automated rollback we had configured to fall back to hosted Redwood model variants didn't trigger because the rollback automation requires both a circuit-breaker trip and a config flag that was accidentally set to false in our canary config.
[02:42] Tom: Ugh, yeah that was a config drift from our rollout last week.
[02:46] Maya: OK this is useful. Let's talk about triage items: first, metric ingestion visibility — we should add a low-latency stream for critical SLO metrics that feeds the circuit-breaker directly with <10s windows. Evan, is that something Redwood can help with?
[03:00] Evan: Yes — we can provide a small telemetry agent snippet you can run near the app to push p95/err rates to our smart routing service. It uses a UDP fire-and-forget and backs off, but gives near real-time signals. We'll share the snippet and a small config.
[03:14] Priya: That would be helpful, though we want that data to remain in house — is there a way to run the agent in our VPC/private deployment?
[03:22] Evan: Absolutely, the telemetry agent can be deployed in your VPC and only posts to the internal control plane endpoint you configure; no logs leave your infra.
[03:32] Daniel: Second, the routing/healthcheck policy — seems like the routing avoids a node after 2 failures; maybe we should use a gradual weight shift with canary instead of hard reject.
[03:42] Maya: We recommend a weighted shift with short-circuit fallback: start at 10% to dedicated, if errors persist raise to 50% over 30s, else fallback to cache. That reduces oscillation.
[03:52] Priya: Makes sense, but we need to ensure the dedicated pool has memory headroom; otherwise we'll just propagate the GC.
[03:58] Evan: Right — recommended step: add a readiness backoff to avoid immediate restarts, and a memory pressure alert before killing. The sequence: detect mem pressure -> signal for graceful model reload or reduce batch size -> if unresolved, mark node draining so router can shift traffic gracefully.
[04:16] Tom: About the rollback config flag — can you explain how Redwood's rollback automation expects signals? We want to avoid config drift causing similar failures.
[04:24] Maya: The automation listens for an 'SLO breach' signal plus a guard check (like canary_enabled) and a heartbeat from your control plane. If any guard is false we don't auto-rollback. We can help set a safe fallback guard that is toggled by a single source-of-truth (e.g., a config stored in your org KMS) so rollouts don't drift.
[04:40] Priya: If we centralize that guard in our KMS-protected config, who's authorized to toggle it? We need RBAC.
[04:47] Evan: You can integrate with SSO/SAML and RBAC. Our control plane honors SAML groups and KMS-enforced secrets. We'll send the RBAC mapping doc.
[04:56] Daniel: Another ask: can we add a 'dry-run' webhook so that when automation would have rolled back, we get a webhook to our incident pipeline for manual override?
[05:04] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports a webhook audit for automation events. We can configure dry-run webhooks to post to your PagerDuty/Slack channel.
[05:12] Tom: Alright, let's pivot to telemetry gaps — Priya mentioned timestamp drift, which makes correlating traces hard.
[05:18] Priya: Our inference nodes were 1.2s skewed from app servers; when events came in metrics ingestion compared them and saw older timestamps so the breaker logic filtered them out.
[05:28] Evan: We should add a synthetic heartbeat that includes monotonic counters so circuit-breaker logic uses sequence gaps instead of wall clock timestamps. That reduces time-drift sensitivity.
[05:38] Maya: Good call. We'll include a sample counter implementation in the telemetry snippet.
[05:44] Daniel: Regarding the runbook — current oncall steps are manual: check metrics pipeline, SSH into node, restart container. Can we automate the first two? 
[05:54] Priya: We'd love to automate checks up to the decision point, but keep a manual confirmation for destructive actions like restart.
[06:02] Evan: We can provide a playbook automation that performs checks (metric backlog, readiness, mem pressure) and posts a recommendation with a one-click restart button to your ops UI. It will not auto-restart unless you flip the consent toggle.
[06:14] Tom: That meets our compliance needs. 
[06:18] Maya: Speaking of compliance — you mentioned KMS and RBAC earlier. Any regulatory approvals needed before we add telemetry agents?
[06:26] Daniel: We're under PCI scope for payment processing, but the recommender is outside PCI; still want to ensure PCI-safer practices. Our security team will want an architecture doc and SOC2 evidence.
[06:36] Evan: We'll send a security pack (SOC2 report, data flow diagrams, minimal data retention config). We'll also highlight that the telemetry agent can redact identifiers and never send user PII.
[06:46] Priya: Good.
[06:48] 
[06:50] — brief screen-share noises, someone shares a link —
[07:05] Maya: I dropped the short decision table in chat: immediate fixes (metric stream + telemetry agent), medium (routing weight policy + readiness backoff), long (runbook automation + dry-run webhooks + RBAC guard centralization).
[07:18] Daniel: For near-term, can you help us run a fire drill in our staging during next week's promo sim? We want to see the breaker and fallback path.
[07:26] Evan: Yes — we can schedule a 60-minute drill. We'll run the sim, flip mem pressures, emulate metric lag, and test your manual approval flow.
[07:36] Maya: Who's the owner for scheduling?
[07:38] Daniel: I'll coordinate with Priya.
[07:40] Priya: OK, I'll block time.
[07:42] Tom: One last thing — do we have an estimate for work effort?
[07:46] Evan: Rough breakdown: telemetry agent + config — 2 dev days + 1 day infra; routing policy changes + readiness tuning — 3 dev days; runbook automation + webhooks — 5 dev days; security pack and RBAC mapping — 2 days. So 13 dev-days total, spread across 2 weeks if we parallelize.
[08:04] Maya: Great. Let's recap final decisions and next steps.
[08:10] (crosstalk)
[08:12] Maya: Recap: Redwood will provide telemetry agent, sample config for canary guard stored in KMS, RBAC mapping doc, webhook dry-run config, and a playbook automation template. HeliosCart will: collect and share filtered traces from the incident, schedule staging fire drill, and centralize the rollback guard in KMS. We'll run a followup to validate.
[08:30] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[08:34] Daniel: Appreciate it.
[08:36] Maya: I'll send notes and the proposed timeline.
[08:40] End of recording.

HeliosCart to gather and upload filtered traces and metric backlog for 2026-05-12 incident
Schedule staging fire drill next week (Daniel/Priya to propose times)
Redwood to send RBAC/KMS integration doc and security pack (SOC2, dataflow)
